title: Options on a game
objectives: Quote calls, puts and straddles on a dice sum, and keep them consistent by parity.

screens.title: A call on two dice
screens.prose: A call with strike 7 pays $S - 7$ when the sum $S$ of two dice is above 7, and nothing otherwise. A sum of 8 pays 1, a sum of 12 pays 5.
screens.question: What is the 7-call worth? Give 4 places.

hints.text: Weight each payoff by its number of rolls out of 36.
8 pays 1 on 5 rolls, 9 pays 2 on 4 rolls, and so on.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the payoff over all 36 rolls.

byKey.zero: You put the average sum, 7, into the payoff. The average of the payoff is not the payoff of the average.
byKey.chance: That is the chance the call pays, 15/36. It pays more than 1 when it pays.
byKey.cond: That is the average payoff when it pays. Weight by the 15/36 chance too.

explain.text: Payoffs 1 to 5 come on 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 rolls: a total of 35 over 36 rolls. The call is worth $35/36 = 0.97$. An option's value is the expectation of its payoff.

screens.title: Put and straddle
screens.prose: A 7-put pays $7 - S$ when $S$ is below 7. The dice are symmetric about 7. A straddle is a call and a put together: it pays $|S - 7|$.
screens.question: What is the 7-straddle worth? Give 4 places.

widget.accept: 35/18 = 1.9444: the call plus the put, each 35/36.
widget.label: Fair value

hints.text: What is the 7-put worth, by symmetry?
The put is a mirror of the call: 35/36.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the call and the put.

byKey.one: That is the call alone. Add the put.
byKey.zero: You priced it at the average sum. The straddle pays on both sides.

explain.text: The put mirrors the call, so it is also worth 35/36. The straddle is $35/18 = 1.94$, which is $E|S - 7|$. It pays most at 2 and 12, where it pays 5.

screens.title: Parity
screens.prose: A call less a put at strike $K$ pays $S - K$ on every roll. So their prices differ by $E[S] - K = 7 - K$. The 8-call is worth $5/9 = 0.5556$.
screens.question: What is the 8-put worth? Give 4 places.

hints.text: Call − put = 7 − 8.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use call − put = 7 − 8 = −1.

byKey.sign: You reversed parity, put − call = 7 − K. It is call − put.
byKey.same: You priced the put like the call. At strike 8 the put is the dearer one.

explain.text: $P = 5/9 + 1 = 14/9 = 1.56$. Above 7, puts are dearer than calls by $K - 7$. Parity fixes one price from the other and the sum.

screens.title: Dealing the straddle
screens.prose: You make the market in the 7-straddle for 2 at a time, width 0.2 to 0.4, limit 4. Skew 0.05 for each straddle you hold. On turn 4 a trader who has seen the first die, listed as `scripted`, may sell to you.
screens.question: Finish the six turns with a P&L of at least £1.50 and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: A market in the 7-straddle on the sum of two dice: it pays $|S - 7|$. Fair is $35/18 = 1.94$. Other traders deal only within 0.3 of fair.
The first die shows 4. The straddle now pays $|D - 3|$ on the second die $D$: fair $9/6 = 1.5$.

hints.text: When the first die shows, what is the straddle worth?
After a 4 it pays $|D - 3|$: fair 1.5.
Quote 1.8 at 2.0 for three turns, then 1.5 at 1.7 after the die.

feedback.correct: You moved with the die and kept edge.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move your quote to the new fair value when the die shows.

byKey.low: Your P&L is under £1.50. A stale bid after the die buys from a trader who knows it is worth 1.5.
byKey.crossed: Your bid met or passed your ask, so nobody traded.
byKey.limit: Your size took you past 4 straddles on one side.

explain.text: The model bought 1 at 1.8, sold 3 at 2.0 and, after the die, bought 1 at 1.5. Short 1 with cash +£2.70 settled at $|8 - 7| = 1$: +£1.70. The stale 1.8 bid was hit for 2 by the trader who saw the 4.

screens.title: Had the die been a 6
screens.prose: You finished holding {{carry.strad.position|0}} straddles, with a P&L in pounds of {{carry.strad.pnl|0}}. The model run ended short 1 with cash +£2.70. The dice were 4 and 4, so it paid 1.

state.caption: Turn 4: the informed sale missed the 1.5 bid.

screens.question: Had the second die been a 6, what would the model run's P&L be, in pounds?

hints.text: The straddle would pay $|4 + 6 - 7| = 3$.
Short 1 owes 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cash 2.70 less a payout of 3.

byKey.sign: You added the payout. Short 1 owes it.

explain.text: With a 6 the straddle pays 3, and short 1 owes it: $2.70 - 3 = -0.30$. That is £2 less than the +£1.70, one for each extra point paid. A short straddle loses when the dice land far from 7.

screens.title: Worth nothing?
screens.prose: A colleague says: "The sum averages 7, so a 7-call pays $7 - 7 = 0$ on average. It is worth nothing."
screens.question: What is wrong with that?

options.text: The call pays on high sums and never below zero, so its average is positive
Nothing: at the money, a call is worth 0
options.why: You priced the payoff of the average sum. The average of the payoff is 35/36.

options.text: The put is worth 0, so the call is worth 7
options.why: You misused parity. Call − put = 7 − 7 = 0, so they are equal, both 35/36.

options.text: It is worth half the sum's sd
options.why: A rule of thumb is not the value. Average the payoff: 35/36.

hints.text: Does the call ever pay a negative amount?
It pays 0 below 7 and up to 5 above.
Average the payoff, not the sum: 35/36.

feedback.correct: The payoff is never negative, so its average is positive.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the call's payoff, not the sum.

byKey.right: You priced the payoff of the average sum. The average of the payoff is 35/36.
byKey.parity: You misused parity. Call − put = 7 − 7 = 0, so they are equal, both 35/36.

explain.text: $(E[S] - 7)^+ = 0$, but $E[(S - 7)^+] = 35/36$. The call keeps the high sums and drops the low ones. That asymmetry is what an option is worth.

screens.title: Quotes that break parity
screens.prose: The interviewer quotes the 7-call at 1.1 to 1.2 and the 7-put at 0.7 to 0.8. The sum itself is 6.9 to 7.1. Sell the call, buy the put, buy the sum: the position pays 7 on every roll.
screens.question: What do you lock in per set, in pounds?

hints.text: What does short call, long put, long sum pay?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The position pays 7; subtract its cost of 6.8.

byKey.cost: That is the cost. The profit is 7 less it.
byKey.mid: You used mid prices. You trade at the quotes.

explain.text: Short call plus long put pays $7 - S$, and the sum adds $S$: 7 on every roll. You pay 6.8 for it, so £0.20 is locked. The call was too dear for the put and the sum.

screens.title: After the first die
screens.prose: The first die turns before the second. The tree shows what the 7-call is worth after each first die.
screens.question: After a first die of 6, what is the 7-call worth?

hints.text: With 6 shown, the call pays $6 + D - 7 = D - 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average $D - 1$ over the six faces of the second die.

byKey.full: You used the best case, a second 6. Average all six faces.
byKey.before: That is the value before the first die.

explain.text: After a 6 the call pays $D - 1$, worth 2.5; after a 1 it cannot pay. The six branch values average back to 35/36. A seller of the call is most exposed after a high first die.

screens.title: Short straddles
screens.prose: You sold 10 straddles at strike 7 for 2.0 each. The dice show 5 and 6.
screens.question: What is your P&L, in pounds?

hints.text: Each straddle pays $|11 - 7| = 4$.
You took in 2.0 and owe 4 on each.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. You owe 4 on each of 10, against 2.0 taken in.

byKey.one: That is one straddle. You sold 10.
byKey.sign: You owe the payout, so the sign is negative.

explain.text: Each straddle owes 4 against 2.0 received: −£2, times 10. The worst rolls, 2 and 12, owe 5 each: −£30. The short straddle gains only on sums 6 to 8, 16 rolls in 36, and loses on 12 rolls in 36.

screens.title: Value and parity
screens.prose:
An option's fair value is the expectation of its payoff. On the two-dice sum, with no time to discount,
$$C_K - P_K = E[S] - K = 7 - K.$$
screens.question: The 9-put is worth $41/18$. What is the 9-call worth? Give 4 places.

byKey.sign: You added 2. The call at 9 is cheaper than the put.

explain.text: $C_9 = 41/18 - 2 = 5/18$, the same as the 5-put by symmetry. Parity lets one quote check another. Any gap is a trade, as the quotes that broke parity showed.

screens.prose: Code the value of any call, put or straddle on the sum over the 36 rolls. Then code the parity check on three quotes.
screens.question: Complete `option_value` and `parity_gap`.

screens.title: Index options
screens.prose: An options market maker sees an index future at 4,000. The 4,000 call is quoted 120 to 122 and the 4,000 put 116 to 118. Take no account of interest.
screens.question: Sell the call, buy the put and buy the future. What is locked per unit, in index points?

hints.text: Short call and long put pay $4{,}000 - S$; the long future pays $S - 4{,}000$.
Together they pay 0 on every outcome.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The legs pay 0 together; count the option cash.

byKey.mids: You used mid prices. Sell at the bid, buy at the ask.
byKey.none: The legs cancel, but the cash does not: +120 − 118.

explain.text: The legs cancel on every outcome, and the options bring in a net 2 points. Market makers keep calls, puts and the future in line so that gaps like this do not appear. When one does, someone trades it at once.

ideas: An option's value is the expectation of its payoff: the 7-call on two dice is worth 35/36.
Parity ties calls, puts and the sum: $C_K - P_K = 7 - K$, and quotes that break it lock a profit.
A short straddle gains near the middle and owes most at the extremes; a revealed die moves every option.

quiz.prose: Two dice. A call with strike 9 pays $S - 9$ when the sum is above 9.
quiz.question: What is it worth? Give 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sums 10, 11, 12 pay 1, 2, 3 on 3, 2, 1 rolls.

byKey.chance: That is the chance it pays, 6/36.

explain.text: $(3 + 4 + 3)/36 = 10/36 = 5/18$. The 5-put is the mirror and has the same value. Calls struck well above 7, and puts well below it, are cheap.

quiz.prose: A call on the two-dice sum with strike 2.
quiz.question: What is it worth?

widget.accept: 5: it always pays S − 2, and E[S] − 2 = 5.
widget.label: Value

feedback.generic: Not quite right. It pays $S - 2$ on every roll.

byKey.zero: You treated 2 as out of the money. Every sum is at least 2.
byKey.seven: That is the sum itself. Subtract the strike.

explain.text: The sum is never below 2, so the call always pays $S - 2$, worth $7 - 2 = 5$. Its put is worth 0, and parity holds: $5 - 0 = 7 - 2$. At strike 12 the call is worth 0.

quiz.prose: A straddle with strike 8 on the two-dice sum.
quiz.question: What is it worth? Give 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the 8-call and the 8-put.

byKey.strad7: That is the 7-straddle. Moving the strike off the centre raises the value.

explain.text: $5/9 + 14/9 = 19/9 = 2.11$. It is dearer than the 7-straddle, because 8 is off the centre of the sum. The straddle is cheapest at the middle strike.
